11: ---
12: 
13: ## 1. Summary
14: 
15: **Verdict: feasible, and worth doing.** SPEC v0.3 is already harness-neutral at its core. The pipeline, claim store, views, job table, tick, MCP pull tools and data directory all carry over unchanged. What differs is a thin adapter layer:
16: 
17: - where transcripts live and how they're parsed;
18: - how hook events map onto the delivery triggers;
19: - which headless command runs housekeeping;
20: - where reports appear;
21: - what schedules the tick;
22: - how the plugin is packaged.
23: 
24: The two harnesses are complementary rather than equivalent:
25: 
26: | | Antigravity | Claude Code |
27: |---|---|---|
28: | **Event path (hooks)** | Adequate but indirect. Hooks mostly re-read the transcript; there's one hook before every model call; `PreToolUse` can only allow/deny/ask. | **Richer.** Hooks receive tool inputs, outputs and errors directly. Context can be injected at prompt submit, before and after tools, after a tool batch, and at subagent start. Async and "rewake" hooks exist. |
29: | **Time path (scheduling)** | **Native.** A plugin sidecar with `builtin: schedule` provides the tick. | **Missing for commands.** Desktop scheduled tasks start full model sessions (fine for reports, not for a one-minute mechanical tick). Cloud routines have no local file access. |
30: | **Headless housekeeping** | `agy -p`, measured at ~17k tokens of fixed overhead and ~13 s per call | `claude -p` with `--safe-mode` and minimal flags, on the subscription. Not yet measured (§4.4). |
31: | **Transcripts** | Pruned by the harness (only 41 of 188 esp32 sessions survive); format undocumented | 30-day default retention; the format is documented as internal and may change between releases |
32: | **Native memory overlap** | Antigravity's `knowledge/` store is empty (unused) | **Auto memory is active.** 13 files for esp32-app-foundation, written by the working agent and loaded every session. |
33: 
34: **The main reason to support both** is that esp32-app-foundation is worked on in both harnesses (188 top-level Antigravity sessions and 35 Claude Code sessions since May). A dead-end found in one should be delivered in the other. A shared claim store gives that for free.
35: 
36: **Recommendation:**
37: 
38: 1. Build one core with a defined adapter interface (§6).
39: 2. Preserve Claude Code history from P0 with a sweep-only copy of its transcripts (SPEC §18.6, rule 11). Both harnesses lose transcripts, so this can't wait for Release 2. The Claude Code adapter itself is Release 2 (R2.1–R2.3).
40: 3. Build delivery on Antigravity first (Release 1), because it's the primary harness by volume. Keep Claude Code's richer hooks as the design check: the capability flags in SPEC §18.3 are how the delivery policy stays harness-neutral.
41: 4. On Claude Code, make the harness's own async hooks trigger the existing tick, keeping the "enqueue, then tick" model you preferred (§4.3).

64: ## 3. Mapping the design onto Claude Code
65: 
66: ### 3.1 Capture
67: 
68: | Need | Claude Code mechanism | Notes |
69: |---|---|---|
70: | Know a session turn ended | `Stop` hook (`session_id`, `transcript_path`, `last_assistant_message`); `SubagentStop` for subagents | Equivalent to Antigravity `Stop`. Spool the entry and copy the transcript, as in SPEC §6.2. |
71: | Session fully ended | `SessionEnd` hook | Only a **1.5 s shared budget** by default. Too tight for anything but writing a spool file; don't copy large transcripts here. |
72: | Transcript location | `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl`; subagents in `<session-id>/subagents/*.jsonl` (17 such files for esp32 on this machine) | The sweep must include the subagent files. PA workers spawned with the `Agent` tool live there. |
73: | Retention | `cleanupPeriodDays`, default **30 days** | Same urgency as Antigravity. On this machine the oldest esp32 transcript is from 19 August, so the sweep hasn't strictly removed everything past 30 days. Capture still shouldn't rely on it. |
74: | Format | JSONL. The docs say *"the entry format is internal to Claude Code and changes between versions"* | The Claude parser must be version-aware and tolerant (§5.1). |
75: | Commit linkage | Same as the spec (git log/reflog by time and branch) | Hook inputs include `tool_input`, so a `PostToolUse` matcher on `Bash` can record commit commands precisely. |
76: 
77: ### 3.2 Delivery
78: 
79: | Trigger (spec §7) | Antigravity (spec v0.3) | Claude Code | Difference |
80: |---|---|---|---|
81: | Always-on map | Include in `GEMINI.md`/`AGENTS.md` | `@.memory/views/MAP.md` import in `CLAUDE.md` (imports recurse up to four hops) | esp32's `CLAUDE.md` already imports `AGENTS.md`. The **include syntax differs**, so each harness's map line goes in its own override file (`GEMINI.md` and `CLAUDE.md`), not the shared `AGENTS.md`. |
82: | Task brief | `PreInvocation` at `invocationNum == 0`, reading the first user message from the transcript | `UserPromptSubmit` receives `prompt` directly and returns `additionalContext` (30 s default timeout) | Claude is simpler and fires for every prompt, so a change of task direction can refresh the brief |
83: | File touch | `PreInvocation` reads the transcript tail for touched paths | `PostToolUse` with `tool_name`/`tool_input` (e.g. `Read`, `Edit`, `Write`) → `additionalContext` | No transcript parsing on the hot path |
84: | Error | `PreInvocation` scans the transcript tail for error text | `PostToolUseFailure` (`error`) and `PostToolUse` (`tool_response`, e.g. a failed build's output) → `additionalContext` | Direct and immediate |
85: | Risky action | `PreToolUse` "gate-once": deny with a reason, allow on re-issue | `PreToolUse` can return `additionalContext` **without blocking**, or `deny`/`ask` with `permissionDecisionReason`; `if` conditions such as `Bash(pio run *)` narrow the matcher | Soft delivery doesn't need the gate-once round-trip. Keep `deny` for hard gates. |
86: | Déjà-vu tier 1 (lexical) | `PreToolUse` on arguments; `PreInvocation` on the latest reasoning | `PreToolUse` on `tool_input`; `PostToolBatch` (after a batch of tool calls, before the next model call) reads the reasoning from the transcript tail | `PostToolBatch` is the nearest equivalent of `PreInvocation` |
87: | Déjà-vu tier 2 (semantic) | Spool, next tick, next `PreInvocation` (≤ ~75 s) | An **`asyncRewake`** command hook runs the check in the background and, on exit code 2, wakes Claude with the alert as a system reminder. Alternatives: a plugin **monitor** streams alerts, or a `prompt`-type hook runs the check in-line. | Claude Code can push asynchronously without waiting for a tick (§4.3) |
88: | Subagent briefing | Unknown whether subagents fire hooks (E8); the fallback is WORKORDER embedding | `SubagentStart` returns `additionalContext` to the new subagent; hooks inside subagents carry `agent_id`/`agent_type` | PA workers get their brief automatically, and are covered by touch, error and déjà-vu delivery |
89: | Pull tools | Plugin MCP server | Plugin `.mcp.json`, same server | Claude Code can defer MCP tool schemas until searched (this session shows it), which lowers the standing context cost |

91: ### 3.3 Time path, executors and visibility
92: 
93: | Need | Claude Code option | Assessment |
94: |---|---|---|
95: | Periodic mechanical tick | No native command scheduler. Options: **async hooks** trigger `repo-memory tick` in the background (§4.3); an **OS scheduler** entry; or the **Antigravity sidecar** if both are installed on the machine. | Async hooks are harness-level and keep the tick as the single executor. Ticks only happen while Claude sessions are active, which is when new work appears anyway. |
96: | Desktop local scheduled task | Starts a full Claude session on a schedule (minimum 1 minute), only while the desktop app is open and the machine is awake. Visible under **Scheduled**. | **Wrong for the tick** (a model session per tick). **Right for reports** (§3.4). |
97: | Cloud routines | Run in the cloud on a fresh clone (minimum 1 hour); no access to local transcripts or the private data directory | Not usable for capture or processing |
98: | `/loop` | Session-scoped polling | Not suitable |
99: | Housekeeping runs | `claude -p` (non-bare, so it uses the subscription login) with `--safe-mode`, `--tools ""`, `--system-prompt-file`, `--json-schema`, `--output-format json`, `--no-session-persistence`, `--model haiku`, `--max-turns`, `--permission-prompts none` | See §4.4. `--bare` would be leaner but **requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`**, which your quota-only constraint rules out. |
100: | Report conversations | Desktop local scheduled task (weekly, visible), or a background session (`claude --bg`, shown in agent view) | Matches the visibility policy (§3.4) |
101: 
102: ### 3.4 The visibility policy on Claude Code
103: 
104: | Class | Antigravity | Claude Code |
105: |---|---|---|
106: | **Repo work** (visible) | IDE sessions, PA workers, bug-fixer loop | Desktop/CLI sessions and their subagents; all appear in the session list |
107: | **Reports** (visible) | `agentapi` conversation titled `[repo-memory] …` | A **Desktop local scheduled task**, e.g. "repo-memory weekly review", appears under **Scheduled** with a notification. The session reads the prepared review (`views/`, `QUESTIONS.md`, pending claims) and you answer there; the sweep captures your replies as evidence. |
108: | **Housekeeping** (hidden) | `agy -p` in a dedicated directory and project; recorded in the CLI store only | `claude -p --no-session-persistence`: **no transcript is written at all**, and `-p` sessions are excluded from the session picker and from `claude --continue` anyway |
109: 
110: Claude Code's hidden path is cleaner than Antigravity's. With `--no-session-persistence` there is nothing to exclude from capture. With `--safe-mode`, no plugins or hooks load inside the run, so recursion is impossible and the `REPO_MEMORY_HOUSEKEEPING` environment guard is belt-and-braces rather than essential.
111: 
112: Desktop scheduled tasks have two caveats:
113: - **Permissions.** A run in Manual permission mode stalls on the first unapproved tool. Set the report task's permission mode and "always allow" the memory MCP tools on the first run.
114: - **Missed runs.** Only one catch-up run happens after sleep.

118: ## 4. The differences that matter, in depth
119: 
120: ### 4.1 Claude Code's event path is the better one
121: 
122: Three properties make the Claude adapter simpler and more precise than the Antigravity one:
123: 
124: 1. **Hook inputs carry the payload.** `PostToolUse` receives `tool_input` and `tool_response`; `PostToolUseFailure` receives `error`; `UserPromptSubmit` receives `prompt`. Antigravity's `PostToolUse` gets only `stepIdx` and `error`, and its `PreInvocation` must re-read the transcript on every model call. On Claude Code the hot path rarely touches the transcript at all.
125: 2. **Context injection is available at the right moments.** `additionalContext` is honoured on `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `PostToolBatch`, `SubagentStart` and `SessionStart`. Antigravity has a single injection point: `ephemeralMessage` at `PreInvocation`, whose persistence is still unknown (E1).
126: 3. **Subagents are first-class.** Hooks fire inside subagents with `agent_id`, and `SubagentStart` can brief them. This closes the gap the spec flags as E8 for Antigravity. Every PA worker on Claude Code gets the task brief and in-session delivery without the PA embedding anything.
127: 
128: **Latency is managed differently.** Claude Code has no hook before every model call; `PostToolUse` fires per tool call instead, at a comparable frequency. The spec's hook-latency budget (§7.8) still applies. Default hook timeouts are generous (600 s; 30 s for `UserPromptSubmit`), but hooks still block, so the fast-path targets stand.
129: 
130: ### 4.2 The time path is Claude Code's gap
131: 
132: Claude Code can run **commands** only in response to events. Its schedulers (Desktop scheduled tasks, cloud routines, `/loop`) all run **model sessions**. There is no equivalent of Antigravity's `builtin: schedule` sidecar. Three workable answers, in order of preference:
133: 
134: 1. **Antigravity's tick serves both** on machines where both harnesses are installed, as on this machine. Claude Code only needs capture and delivery hooks, because the tick processes the shared queue.
135: 2. **Async hooks as tick triggers** (§4.3) on Claude Code-only machines. Processing happens while Claude sessions are active. Calendar jobs (daily publish, weekly review) run at the first tick after they fall due.
136: 3. **An OS scheduler entry** (`repo-memory schedule install`: launchd, cron or Task Scheduler), added only if calendar jobs must run when no session is open.
137: 
138: ### 4.3 Claude Code has harness-level async, so the tick model survives
139: 
140: Claude Code documents two background hook modes for command hooks:
141: 
142: | Field | Behaviour |
143: |---|---|
144: | `async: true` | Runs in the background without blocking. Output is discarded, and the hook's timeout isn't enforced. |
145: | `asyncRewake: true` | Runs in the background. On **exit code 2**, Claude is woken and the hook's stderr is shown to it as a system reminder. |
146: 
147: This is the harness-supervised async we looked for in Antigravity and didn't find. It fits your preference for "enqueue, then tick" without inventing a second executor:
148: 
149: - **The tick stays the only thing that does work.** An async hook runs `repo-memory tick`, the same entry point the Antigravity sidecar runs. It's just another trigger. `tick.lock` makes redundant triggers no-ops.
150: - **Suggested triggers:**
151:   - `Stop` with `async: true`: process the finished turn's spool promptly;
152:   - `SessionStart` with `async: true`: catch up on anything missed while no session was running.
153: - **Déjà-vu tier 2 uses `asyncRewake`.**
154:   1. A `PostToolBatch` hook spools a check request and starts an `asyncRewake` hook that runs the tick's interactive step for that one request.
155:   2. If the tick finds a match, the hook exits 2 with the alert text.
156:   3. Claude is woken with the alert as a system reminder. That takes seconds, where Antigravity has to wait up to a minute for the next tick.
157: - **Plugin monitors** are an alternative push channel: a background process per interactive session whose output reaches Claude as notifications. They're marked experimental and don't run in `-p` sessions or on Bedrock, Google Cloud or Foundry, so they're a second choice after `asyncRewake`.
158: 
159: **Open question C3:** does an async hook's process survive the end of the session or the app quitting? If not, work still completes on the next trigger, because jobs are durable (spec §4.3).
160: 
161: ### 4.4 Headless housekeeping on the Claude subscription
162: 
163: The candidate invocation for a pure-function pipeline stage:
164: 
165: ```
166: claude -p --safe-mode \
167:   --system-prompt-file <stage>.system.md --tools "" \
168:   --json-schema "$(cat <stage>.schema.json)" --output-format json \
169:   --model haiku --max-turns 1 \
170:   --no-session-persistence --permission-prompts none \
171:   < payload
172: ```
173: 
174: The flags do the following:
175: 
176: | Flag | Effect |
177: |---|---|
178: | `--safe-mode` | Skips `CLAUDE.md`, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers and auto memory while keeping **normal authentication**, so it works on the subscription. `--bare` also skips all of that but needs an API key. |
179: | `--system-prompt-file`, `--tools ""` | Replace the coding-agent prompt and remove tools. This is the main lever on fixed overhead. |
180: | `--json-schema` + `--output-format json` | Validated output in `structured_output`, plus `usage` and `total_cost_usd` for the metrics store (spec §10.4) |
181: | `--no-session-persistence` | Nothing is written to disk |
182: | Piped stdin | Capped at 10 MB, far above the per-call payload targets |
183: 
184: Status and prerequisites:
185: - **Not measured.** On this machine, the CLI bundled with the desktop app (`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude-code/2.1.284/…/claude`) reports *Not logged in*: the desktop app's sign-in doesn't carry over to the standalone CLI. Measuring needs you to run `claude auth login` (or `claude setup-token` for a long-lived token for scheduled use). That's experiment C1.
186: - **Expected overhead.** Because the default system prompt and tools can be replaced outright, which `agy -p` doesn't allow, fixed overhead should be well below the ~17k measured for `agy -p`. C1 will confirm or refute that.
187: - **Whose quota.** You've asked for the Antigravity quota. On machines with both harnesses, housekeeping therefore uses `agy -p`, and `claude -p` is the executor only on Claude Code-only machines. It's one setting (`housekeeping.executor: agy | claude`), and every call's usage is recorded, so the choice can be revisited with data.
188: 
189: ### 4.5 Transcript stability is Claude Code's biggest engineering risk
190: 
191: Anthropic documents the transcript JSONL as internal and version-dependent, and recommends `/export`, `claude -p --resume … --output-format json`, hooks or the Agent SDK instead. None of those give a complete, structured history of an *interactive* session after the fact, so parsing the JSONL remains the practical route. Mitigations:
192: 
193: - **Tolerant parser.** Keep a narrow dependency on the stable essentials (role, text, thinking, tool use/result, timestamps, `isSidechain`/subagent linkage), with unknown entry types ignored rather than fatal.
194: - **Version detection.** Record the Claude Code version per episode, and keep a fixture corpus of real transcripts per version. A canary test runs on each Claude Code update and flags any drop in parsed-step counts.
195: - **Belt and braces from hooks.** The hot path already sees tool inputs, outputs and errors. The `Stop` hook can append those essentials to a harness-neutral side-log, so a parser break loses less.
196: - **Retention.** Capture within the 30-day window. Optionally raise `cleanupPeriodDays` for repositories using the plugin, as a user choice.
197: 
198: ### 4.6 Coexisting with Claude Code's auto memory
199: 
200: Auto memory is on by default. For esp32-app-foundation it holds 13 files, and its `MEMORY.md` index is loaded into every Claude Code session (first 200 lines or 25 KB). It overlaps directly with repo memory:
201: 
202: | | Claude Code auto memory | Repo memory (this plugin) |
203: |---|---|---|
204: | Written by | The working agent, in-session (costs main-session tokens) | The pipeline, from transcripts (the working agent writes nothing) |
205: | Scope | Per user and machine; not shared, not in git | Per repository; shared via git after review |
206: | Content today (esp32) | Personal workflow preferences (worker spawn mode) **and** repo knowledge ("portal assets: native stub shadowing", "CrowPanel PWR_EN bring-up", "BLE RFC #225 lead suspect") | Repo knowledge with evidence, anchors and status |
207: | Validation | None; the `modified` timestamp only | Anchors, re-checks on change, trust ladder |
208: | Reaches subagents | No (main conversation only) | Yes, via `SubagentStart` |
209: 
210: Recommended coexistence:
211: 1. **Import auto memory as evidence.** Treat each auto-memory file as an import episode (`provenance: claude-auto-memory`). `feedback` entries are human-stated. `project` and `reference` entries become `observed` candidates, verified like any other claim. Several esp32 entries (native stub shadowing, CrowPanel bring-up) are exactly the gotchas the claim store should hold and share.
212: 2. **Steer, don't disable.** Add a line to `CLAUDE.md`: repository knowledge is captured automatically by repo-memory, so auto memory should keep to personal preferences. Leave `autoMemoryEnabled` as your choice.
213: 3. **Never write into auto memory** from the plugin. It's the user's private store.
214: 
215: Item 1 is refined in §4.7 (Claude-specific note 2).
216: 
217: ### 4.7 Lessons from auto memory
218: 
219: Auto memory is the opposite design to repo memory. The working agent writes notes during the session, nothing processes them afterwards, and nothing re-checks them. A review of how it works, and of what it holds for esp32-app-foundation, found techniques worth reusing. The harness-neutral ones were adopted in SPEC v0.5. This section keeps the Claude-specific detail for the P2 adapter.
220: 
221: #### How it works
222: 
223: | Aspect | Behaviour |
224: |---|---|
225: | Storage | `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/`, one directory per git repository (shared across worktrees). `autoMemoryDirectory` moves it; `autoMemoryEnabled: false` or `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` turns it off. Excluded from the transcript retention sweep. |
226: | Unit | One fact per file. Frontmatter: `name`, `description`, `metadata.type` (`user`, `feedback`, `project`, `reference`). Claude Code stamps `modified` (ISO 8601) on each write to a file that has frontmatter (v2.1.214+). The esp32 files also carry `originSessionId`. |
227: | Loading | A `MEMORY.md` index, one line per memory. Its first 200 lines or 25 KB load at session start. Topic files are opened on demand with ordinary file tools, and each file's `description` exists to support that choice. Not loaded into subagents, except forks. |
228: | Budget enforcement | After each write to `MEMORY.md` the harness measures the file. Near a limit, it reminds the model to shorten it. Over a limit, the write succeeds but returns an error telling the model to rewrite the index. |
229: | Writing rules (from the agent's instructions) | Skip what the code, git history or `CLAUDE.md` already say. Update an existing file rather than duplicating it; delete memories that prove wrong. Convert relative dates to absolute ones. `feedback` and `project` entries carry **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. `[[name]]` links join related memories; a link to a memory not yet written marks a gap. Save approaches the user confirms, not only corrections. |
230: | Reading rules | Recalled memories are framed as what was true when written. A named file, function or flag must be checked before it is recommended. |
231: | Consolidation | The `consolidate-memory` skill, run on request: merge overlaps, separate durable from dated entries, fix time references, drop what is easy to re-find, and keep the index under 200 lines with entries under ~150 characters. |
232: | Recall | The UI reports "Recalled N memories". None of the 35 esp32 transcripts contains a memory-recall attachment, so on this machine retrieval has been the agent reading the index and opening files itself. |
233: 
234: #### What esp32-app-foundation's auto memory shows (2026-09-30)
235: 
236: - **Content.** There are 12 topic files plus the index: 8 `project`, 3 `feedback`, 1 `reference`. Half carry both Why and How to apply, and those are the most useful. The gotchas are exactly what the claim store wants, such as native stub shadowing and the CrowPanel PWR_EN bring-up.
237: - **Status goes stale.** `ble-manager-rfc-225.md` (modified 2026-09-23 06:55Z) says WO-6 is BLOCKED and the BT-memory-release root cause is unconfirmed on hardware. Its index line says the same, so every session loads it.
238:   - Later on 2026-09-23, `fc974687` ("prevent Arduino BT memory release") fixed that cause, and `eaf236a7` recorded that the WO-6 hardware acceptance tests passed.
239:   - A week later the memory is unchanged.
240: - **Index drift.** The longest index line is 379 characters (hardware-config design status), against the ~150 target.
241: - **Gaps.** One forward link is dangling: `[[bug-fixer-lacks-pa-context]]`.
242: - **Volume.** 12 memories between June and September on the most active repository. Writing memory during the session only happens when the agent notices something.
243: 
244: #### Adopted in SPEC v0.5 (harness-neutral)
245: 
246: | Auto-memory technique | SPEC change |
247: |---|---|
248: | A `description` written for selection; a one-line index; topic files opened on demand | `relevant_when` line; claim index view; the agent walks MAP → index → claim (§5.3, §5.5, §7.2, §7.9) |
249: | **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines | `apply` line, rendered in pushes (§5.3, §7.1, §7.3) |
250: | `modified` stamp; "true when written"; check names before recommending them | A currency stamp on every push; the hook checks that anchored files exist (§7.1) |
251: | Consolidation separates dated from durable entries (and the stale BLE memory above) | `closes_when` on `open-issue`, a `resolved` status, closure evaluated by the tick (§5.3.1, §5.3.2, §8) |
252: | The agent's own "worth remembering" judgement | Memory-artefact writes as a triage keep rule, a salience window and `note` steps (§5.1, §6.4, §6.5) |
253: | Index budget measured by the harness, with a rewrite instruction | Over-budget views are re-synthesised rather than truncated (§6.8) |
254: | Forward links as gap markers | `gaps` from extraction feed coverage (§6.5, §9.1) |
255: | Saving confirmed approaches, not only corrections | Approval signals in triage (§6.4) |
256: 
257: #### Claude-specific notes for Release 2 (R2.1–R2.2)
258: 
259: 1. **Auto memory is a memory artefact.** Add `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/` to the Claude adapter's `triage.memory_artefacts`. Writes to it appear in the transcript as `Write`/`Edit` tool calls with their full text, so compaction turns them into `note` steps without any hook. A real-time `PostToolUse` hook isn't needed.
260: 2. **Import auto memory with exposure awareness.** This refines §4.6 item 1 and SPEC §12.2.2, which treat `feedback` entries as human-stated.
261:    - **The risk.** An auto memory is the agent's paraphrase, so under P13 it is a lead, not evidence. Once delivery pushes claims in Claude Code (R2.2), the agent can restate a pushed claim in auto memory, and importing that memory would support the claim with itself.
262:    - **The rule.**
263:      - Resolve `originSessionId` to the source session's episode, and take evidence from that episode's human-authored steps and tool outcomes.
264:      - If the source transcript is gone, import the memory at most as `observed`, never `confirmed`.
265:      - Check the source episode's exposure steps. A memory written after exposure to a claim that it restates is marked `echo_of`, not support.
266: 3. **Report stale auto memories; don't fix them.** The plugin never writes into auto memory (§4.6). The weekly report can list auto-memory entries that claims or commits contradict (the BLE entry above would qualify) as proposed work for the human. SPEC §9.4 already proposes fixes this way for documents that contradict verified claims.
267: 4. **Subagent memory is a second store, and it lives in the repo.** A subagent definition's `memory` field gives it its own auto memory:
268:    - `user` → `~/.claude/agent-memory/<agent>/`;
269:    - `project` → `.claude/agent-memory/<agent>/`, committed to git (the docs recommend this scope);
270:    - `local` → `.claude/agent-memory-local/<agent>/`.
271: 
272:    Its `MEMORY.md` (200 lines / 25 KB) loads when the subagent starts, and Read, Write and Edit are enabled automatically. If PA workers adopt it:
273:    - treat it as another memory artefact and import source, under the rules in note 2;
274:    - don't generate into it, because the subagent edits it too;
275:    - expect it to overlap with the `SubagentStart` brief, and steer it towards agent-specific working notes in the agent definition, as §4.6 does for auto memory.
276: 
277:    In esp32-app-foundation, `.claude` links to `.agents`, so project-scope files would land in `.agents/agent-memory/`.
278: 5. **Don't copy:**
279:    - writing memory during the session as the main path (it costs main-session tokens and depends on the agent noticing);
280:    - the lack of re-checking;
281:    - a flat 200-line index (fine for dozens of notes, not for thousands of claims);
282:    - loading into the main agent only.

286: ## 5. Engineering notes for the dual-harness core
287: 
288: ### 5.1 Normalised episode input
289: 
290: The spec's episode format (§5.1) is already harness-neutral. The Claude Code parser maps:
291: 
292: | Claude Code JSONL | Episode step |
293: |---|---|
294: | `user` message with text | `user` |
295: | `assistant` text block | `agent` |
296: | `assistant` thinking block | `reasoning` |
297: | `tool_use` + `tool_result` (Bash) | `command` with outcome and error excerpt |
298: | `tool_use` Edit/Write | `edit` (path only) |
299: | `tool_use` Read | `read` (path only) |
300: | Subagent transcript (`subagents/*.jsonl`) | `subagent` → nested episode |
301: 
302: Measured composition for the 35 esp32 Claude Code sessions (spec Appendix A.2): 70% tool traffic, so the spec's compaction target (≥ 3×) applies equally.
303: 
304: ### 5.2 Normalised hook events
305: 
306: Both adapters translate native hook payloads into one internal event model, so delivery logic is written once:
307: 
308: | Normalised event | Antigravity source | Claude Code source |
309: |---|---|---|
310: | `session.turn_end` | `Stop` | `Stop` / `SubagentStop` |
311: | `prompt.submitted` | `PreInvocation` (`invocationNum == 0`) + transcript read | `UserPromptSubmit` |
312: | `tool.proposed` | `PreToolUse` | `PreToolUse` |
313: | `tool.completed` | `PreInvocation` transcript tail (`PostToolUse` has no payload) | `PostToolUse` |
314: | `tool.failed` | `PreInvocation` transcript tail | `PostToolUseFailure` |
315: | `model.about_to_run` | `PreInvocation` | `PostToolBatch` (closest equivalent) |
316: | `subagent.started` | n/a (E8) | `SubagentStart` |
317: 
318: ### 5.3 Injection semantics
319: 
320: | | Antigravity | Claude Code |
321: |---|---|---|
322: | Soft context | `injectSteps` → `ephemeralMessage` (persistence unknown, E1) | `additionalContext` (persistence to be confirmed, C2) |
323: | Block with explanation | `PreToolUse` `deny` + `reason` | `PreToolUse` `permissionDecision: "deny"` + `permissionDecisionReason` |
324: | Ask the human | `ask` / `force_ask` | `ask` |
325: | Async push | None | `asyncRewake` (exit 2 → system reminder); plugin monitors |
326: 
327: The delivery ledger (spec §7.1) dedupes in both, whatever the persistence semantics turn out to be.
328: 
329: ### 5.4 One generated rule file for both harnesses (to test)
330: 
331: In esp32-app-foundation, `.claude` is a symlink to `.agents`, so `.claude/rules/` **is** `.agents/rules/`. That makes a zero-code native delivery floor possible: generate one compact rule per subsystem (invariants, ruled-out approaches, failure signatures; ≤ ~1.5k tokens) into `.agents/rules/`, with frontmatter for both harnesses:
332: 
333: - Claude Code reads only `paths:` and ignores other keys.
334: - Antigravity would read its own glob activation keys.
335: 
336: If each harness ignores the other's keys (experiment C6, alongside the spec's E4), then touching OTA files loads the OTA rule in both harnesses with no hooks running at all.
337: 
338: Two limits:
339: - **Antigravity** scans only immediate children of `.agents/rules/`, so the generated files must sit at the top level.
340: - **Budget.** Unscoped rules load every session in both harnesses. Only path-scoped ones may be generated, to protect the rules budget.
341: 
342: This gives a **degraded mode that works natively in both**: map include + path-scoped rules + MCP pull tools, with no hooks and no tick.

346: ## 6. Recommended dual-harness structure
347: 
348: > Superseded in detail by SPEC §18 (Go package layout, harness interface and capability flags). The structure below remains the conceptual map.
349: 
350: ```
351: repo-memory/                          # one source repository
352: ├── core/                             # harness-neutral: pipeline, claims, views, index,
353: │                                     # job table, tick, MCP server, normalised events
354: ├── adapters/
355: │   ├── antigravity/                  # transcript parser, hook I/O, agy executor,
356: │   │                                 # agentapi reports, sidecar definition
357: │   └── claude_code/                  # transcript parser (versioned), hook I/O,
358: │                                     # claude -p executor, desktop-task reports
359: ├── packaging/
360: │   ├── antigravity-plugin/           # plugin.json, hooks.json, mcp_config.json,
361: │   │                                 # sidecars/tick, rules/, skills/
362: │   └── claude-code-plugin/           # .claude-plugin/plugin.json, hooks/hooks.json,
363: │                                     # .mcp.json, skills/, marketplace entry
364: └── tests/fixtures/{antigravity,claude_code}/<version>/   # transcript corpora
365: ```
366: 
367: **Adapter interface.** Each harness implements the same small set of methods:
368: 
369: | Method | Purpose |
370: |---|---|
371: | `discover_transcripts(since)` | Sweep support |
372: | `parse_transcript(path)` → steps | Parser |
373: | `normalise_hook(event_json)` → event | Hook input |
374: | `render_injection(items)` → output JSON | Hook output |
375: | `run_housekeeping(system, payload, schema, model)` → result + usage | Executor |
376: | `start_report(title, prompt)` → handle | Report surface |
377: | `schedule_install()` | Tick scheduling |
378: 
379: **Per-machine configuration** (`<data-dir>/config.yaml`):
380: - `housekeeping.executor: agy | claude` (default `agy` where Antigravity is installed, per your quota preference);
381: - `reports.surface: antigravity | claude-desktop`;
382: - `tick.trigger: sidecar | async-hooks | os-scheduler` (more than one is allowed; `tick.lock` dedupes).
383: 
384: **Shared data directory.** Both adapters write the same `<data-dir>/<repo-id>/`. Claude Code's `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` (`~/.claude/plugins/data/<id>/`) holds only plugin-installed dependencies, so the two harnesses never split state.

388: ## 7. Feasibility and risks
389: 
390: | Risk | Severity | Mitigation |
391: |---|---|---|
392: | Claude Code transcript format changes between releases (the product ships frequently; 2.1.284 today, and the hook list now has 32 events) | High | Versioned tolerant parser, fixture corpus, canary on update, hook side-log (§4.5) |
393: | No native command scheduler in Claude Code | Medium | Antigravity tick when co-installed; async-hook ticks; optional OS scheduler (§4.2) |
394: | Two authentication setups and two quotas | Medium | One executor per machine, chosen in config. The standalone Claude CLI must be signed in separately from the desktop app (§4.4). |
395: | Different injection semantics (`ephemeralMessage` vs `additionalContext`) | Medium | Normalised injection with ledger dedupe; E1 and C2 settle the semantics |
396: | Auto memory duplicating or contradicting repo memory | Medium | Import as evidence; steer via `CLAUDE.md` (§4.6) |
397: | Auto memory or subagent memory restating pushed claims, then being imported as support for them (circular evidence) | Medium | Exposure-aware import through `originSessionId` (§4.7, note 2); C8 measures how often it happens |
398: | Test matrix: 2 harnesses × 3 OSes × harness versions | Medium | Shared core tested once; adapters tested against fixtures; hook contract tests per harness |
399: | Hook API drift in either harness | Medium | Thin adapters, contract tests, and a `repo-memory doctor` that checks hook registration and delivery end to end |

1: # **Architecting Agentic Memory for Google Antigravity: A Research Survey and Implementation Blueprint**
2: 
3: The evolution of autonomous coding agents has catalyzed a paradigm shift in software engineering, moving the primary operational bottleneck from the reasoning capabilities of large language models to the surrounding harness architecture. Specifically, the challenge lies in how these autonomous systems manage, retrieve, and govern persistent contextual information. Traditional applications operate in a stateless paradigm, treating each developmental session as an isolated event. This leads to redundant discovery, the repetition of previously resolved errors, and the continuous loss of critical architectural decision records. As agents are increasingly tasked with repository-level maintenance, feature extension, and longitudinal project evolution, they require a memory substrate that can persist experience across sessions without overwhelmingly bloating the token context window.  
4: This report presents an exhaustive analysis of agentic memory systems to address the requirement for a repository-level memory plugin operating within the Google Antigravity harness. The objective is to architect a system that scans project conversations, distills architectural decisions, tracks dead-ends, and surfaces this collective experience to developers and agents in future sessions. Crucially, the solution must optimize for token efficiency in both extraction and retrieval, while remaining lightweight, portable, and natively committable to Git version control.
5: 
6: ## **The Pathology of Context Rot and the Necessity of Bounded Memory**
7: 
8: The prevailing assumption in early large language model application design was that increasingly larger context windows would natively solve the memory problem. Empirical evidence demonstrates this to be mathematically and operationally false. Research evaluating extended context limits across frontier models reveals a phenomenon known as context rot, or attention dilution, where model performance consistently degrades as input length increases.  
9: As the context window expands with raw transcript data, the signal-to-noise ratio degrades precipitously. Models exhibit a pronounced positional bias, often referred to as the lost-in-the-middle effect, causing them to overlook critical constraints or instructions buried deep within a session's interaction history. Furthermore, retaining raw conversation logs introduces severe temporal contradictions. An agent might recall that an API endpoint is formatted as a specific version from an early conversation, completely ignoring a recent migration discussed later, simply because the sheer volume of stale facts mathematically dilutes the updated information.  
10: To prevent context rot, modern systems employ a bounded memory architecture where active context is managed dynamically through explicit context engineering. A raw, full-append strategy results in quadratic token cost growth, mathematically expressed as O(n^2), where the computational cost scales with the square of the conversation length. This leads to rapid cost explosion and performance degradation. Conversely, systems employing validated compaction and distillation—where older conversation turns are summarized, evaluated, and explicitly written to an external storage mechanism—achieve stable, linear O(n) scaling. At a benchmark of 500 conversation turns, validated compaction yields an approximate 96 percent token savings compared to naive full-context appending.
11: 
12: ![Image][image1]The architectural transition from transcript replay to semantic distillation is not merely a cost-saving measure; it is a fundamental requirement for autonomous reliability. Relying on raw logs forces the model to constantly re-evaluate contradictions, whereas a distilled memory architecture presents the model with a single, verified truth state.
13: 
14: ## **Architectural Paradigms of Agentic Memory**
15: 
16: The field of agentic memory has rapidly stratified into distinct architectural philosophies, driven by the dual constraints of finite context windows and the computational overhead of continuous data ingestion. Understanding the taxonomy of these systems is a prerequisite for selecting the optimal design pattern for a repository-level integration.  
17: Agent memory is typically categorized across three orthogonal dimensions: the substrate, the cognitive mechanism, and the subject. The substrate dictates where information is held, differentiating between internal memory embedded in model parameters and external memory housed in non-parametric stores like databases or file systems. The subject dimension delineates whether the memory tracks user-centric preferences or agent-centric execution trajectories. Most critically, the cognitive mechanism defines how the memory functions, generally divided into three primary types: episodic, semantic, and procedural.  
18: Episodic memory stores a chronological ledger of past interactions, state transitions, and completed work segments, allowing the agent to reconstruct historical trajectories. Semantic memory abstracts stable facts, concepts, and overarching architectural decisions from specific episodes, enabling generalization beyond a single session. Procedural memory encodes reusable skills, tool execution patterns, and routines that dictate how the agent operates, typically stored as versioned rules. For a software engineering agent, semantic and procedural memories are paramount, as they encapsulate the architectural decision records, the operational guardrails, and the cumulative "gotchas" discovered during development.
19: 
20: ### **History-First vs. Distillation-First Extraction**
21: 
22: The mechanisms by which information is moved from the active context into permanent storage form a major architectural divide. Early frameworks often utilized a history-first architecture, where raw conversation turns were ingested directly into a storage layer, followed by asynchronous entity extraction to build a temporal graph on top of the raw logs. This approach prioritizes data retention but sacrifices retrieval efficiency.  
23: The current state-of-the-art favors distillation-first architectures. In this paradigm, raw turns are never utilized as the foundational unit of storage; instead, the system dynamically extracts, consolidates, and validates discrete facts before they are committed to memory. This ensures that extended periods of low-information conversational static produce zero memory bloat, whereas a single interaction containing a critical architectural decision produces exactly one highly durable memory artifact. Distillation-first architectures require explicit mechanisms for contradiction detection and fact supersession. When an agent learns a new constraint that invalidates a prior assumption, it does not merely append the new fact; it updates or explicitly supersedes the outdated record, thereby maintaining a coherent and unpolluted knowledge base.
24: 
25: ### **The Vector-Graph Tradeoff and Token Economics**
26: 
27: The choice of retrieval mechanism heavily influences both the accuracy and the operational cost of the memory system. While vector-based similarity search excels at semantic matching, it struggles with temporal reasoning and multi-hop entity relationships. This has led to the rise of hybrid systems that combine vector storage with knowledge graphs, though this introduces severe trade-offs in token expenditure during the extraction phase.
28: 
29: | Architecture Type | Representative System | Indexing Cost Profile | Indexing Speed | Key Capabilities and Limitations |
30: | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
31: | Distillation & Hybrid Vector | Mem0 | Low (\$0.01 \- \$0.50 per large corpus) | Real-time / Asynchronous | High temporal F1 score; utilizes key-value stores for metadata and vector search for semantic relevance; minimal token bloat. |
32: | Dense Temporal Graph | Graphiti / GraphRAG | Very High (\$50 \- \$200 per 500 pages) | Slow (\~45 minutes per large batch) | Exceptional multi-hop reasoning and community summarization; massive token consumption due to LLM-powered entity and edge extraction. |
33: | Dual-Level Fast Graph | LightRAG | Very Low (\~\$0.50 per 500 pages) | Fast (\~3 minutes) | Segments documents for quick entity extraction; flat graph structure provides 70-90% of dense graph quality at a fraction of the cost; lacks hierarchical summarization. |
34: | History-First Graph | Zep | Moderate to High | Real-time batching | Strong temporal tracking of entity state changes; raw log retention increases storage footprint and retrieval latency. |
35: 
36: The data indicates that while dense knowledge graphs provide superior global query support, their LLM-driven extraction pipelines consume an exorbitant amount of tokens, frequently negating the efficiency goals of a lightweight agent harness. For a repository-level memory system operating continuously in the background, a distillation-first vector approach augmented with lightweight, flat-graph relationships offers the optimal balance of reasoning capability and financial viability.
37: 
38: ## **The Substrate: Git-Backed, Markdown-Canonical Memory**
39: 
40: While cloud-hosted vector databases and complex graph environments dominate generic enterprise retrieval systems, repository-level coding agents require a fundamentally different storage paradigm. For software engineering, the optimal substrate for an agent's memory is the very environment it operates within: the Git version control system.  
41: Constructing an agent's memory entirely out of plain Markdown files within a dedicated .agents/memory/ directory provides unparalleled transparency, auditability, and durability. Relying on opaque, external vector databases as the primary source of truth introduces unacceptable fragility; the knowledge becomes invisible to human developers, difficult to migrate across workstations, and susceptible to complete loss in the event of database corruption. By treating plain Markdown as the canonical truth, the architecture leverages the inherent strengths of version control.  
42: Temporal provenance is natively resolved by Git operations. The system gains the ability to track exactly how knowledge evolves over time without requiring complex custom temporal graphs. A standard git diff operation instantly reveals how the agent's understanding of an entity changed, git blame exposes the exact timestamp and context of when a specific architectural constraint was learned, and git checkout allows developers to revert the agent's cognitive state to match a historical branch perfectly. Furthermore, the memory travels directly with the code. Fresh clones of the repository immediately contain the accumulated project experience, drastically reducing onboarding time for both human engineers and new autonomous agents, as there is no external database to provision or arbitrate for staleness.  
43: Crucially, this approach enforces human-in-the-loop governance. Human engineers can seamlessly open a Markdown memory file in their integrated development environment, review the agent's assumptions, manually correct a hallucinated fact, and commit the fix alongside application code. The markdown is human-readable, strongly typed by directory structure, and easily governed by standard pull request review processes.
44: 
45: ### **Structuring the Experience Artifacts**
46: 
47: To prevent the accumulation of noise, the memory substrate cannot be a single, monolithic log file. Knowledge must be fragmented into highly structured, discrete artifacts often referred to as Experience Cards. These artifacts are categorized by their cognitive purpose.  
48: Artifacts documenting dead-ends and development "gotchas" are critical. When a specific library upgrade causes a subtle deadlock, the agent documents this failure mode in a dedicated artifact. Future sessions attempting similar tasks will retrieve this card and preemptively avoid the regression, effectively halting the repetition of complex errors. Architectural Decision Records form another core artifact class, establishing explicit rules regarding logging formats, authentication flows, and component hierarchies that the agent must continuously obey. Finally, continuity states track active project facts, complete with metadata footers that record creation dates, usage frequency, and hierarchical tiers, acting as an event-sourced ledger for the project's evolution.
49: 
50: ### **Structural Resolution of Concurrent Write Conflicts**
51: 
52: A well-documented limitation of storing autonomous memory in Git is the high probability of merge conflicts. If multiple developers or parallel subagents generate memories simultaneously on different branches, conventional Git merges will fail when attempting to reconcile concurrent appends to a shared memory index.  
53: The resolution to this challenge involves both topographical design and custom tooling. Topographically, the memory directory must be structured to isolate hot spots, storing each open thread, concept, or entity in its own distinct file rather than appending to a single global ledger. Technically, this is supported by the installation of an AI-aware Git merge driver. Custom drivers intercept merge operations specifically on the memory directory and perform entity-level, section-aware union merges by ID, seamlessly and silently resolving concurrent appends without requiring manual developer intervention.
54: 
55: ## **Optimizing Retrieval: The Embedded Indexing Engine**
56: 
57: A dual-layer architecture separates the durable state, represented by Git-committed Markdown files, from the ephemeral search index, handled by sqlite-vec. This structural division guarantees portability and human readability while simultaneously maintaining sub-50ms hybrid retrieval speeds, ensuring data flows efficiently from the file system into the agent context window. While Markdown files serve as the durable source of truth, an agent cannot efficiently read thousands of files per prompt. A highly optimized, embedded retrieval engine is required to surface only the strictly relevant context.  
58: To maintain the requirement that the system runs entirely within the Google Antigravity plugin harness without external infrastructure, the indexing layer must be tightly embedded.
59: 
60: | Embedded Engine | Core Architecture | Memory Scaling Profile | Primary Use Case and Limitations |
61: | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
62: | sqlite-vec | Pure C virtual table extension for SQLite | Minimal footprint, highly scan-bound | Ideal for zero-dependency local agent plugins. Lacks advanced graph capabilities natively but excels at fast hybrid lexical/vector search on moderate corpora. |
63: | LanceDB | Rust-based, Apache Arrow columnar storage | Disk-first; massive scale with minimal RAM | Best for multi-million vector datasets requiring zero-copy reads. Can be overly heavy for a lightweight IDE plugin. |
64: | DuckDB-VSS | C++ vectorized analytical engine | Memory-resident HNSW index | Highly performant for analytical workloads, but RAM footprint grows significantly with dataset size. |
65: | Chroma (Embedded) | Python/Rust core with SQLite metadata | Memory-resident HNSW index | Standard for Python frameworks, but RAM limits scale, and multi-process concurrency can be problematic. |
66: 
67: The sqlite-vec engine, designed as the pure-C successor to sqlite-vss, represents a watershed capability for local agent memory. It operates as a virtual table within a standard SQLite database, allowing the system to store both full-text data and vector embeddings within a single, atomic transactional boundary. The memory.sqlite file acts purely as an ephemeral, rebuildable index that can be instantly reconstructed from the Markdown substrate if lost or corrupted.  
68: When a session requires context, the system executes a Reciprocal Rank Fusion query that seamlessly combines BM25 lexical scoring from SQLite's full-text search with cosine similarity vector search from sqlite-vec. This hybrid approach drastically improves recall by matching both exact variable names and broad semantic concepts simultaneously.
69: 
70: ### **Hierarchical Code Memory and ContextSniper**
71: 
72: Token efficiency during the retrieval phase is maximized by adopting a hierarchical memory structure, heavily informed by the ContextSniper architecture utilized in advanced repository-repair systems. This paradigm inserts a filtering layer between the agent and the repository, converting noisy data into ultra-compact evidence packets.  
73: The memory is indexed into three distinct levels of granularity. The foundational level is the compact abstract, which contains high-level symbolic metadata, function signatures, and summarized intent. The middle level provides a structured overview, detailing the relationships between components and summarized architectural decisions. The final level contains the verbatim code or the full text of the Markdown document.  
74: When a session begins, the agent injects only the compact abstracts into the active prompt context. If the agent's reasoning dictates that a specific dead-end or architectural rule is highly relevant to the immediate task, it executes a precise tool call to expand that specific artifact into its full content view. This deliberate lazy-loading approach prevents context stuffing, drastically cuts API inference costs, and eliminates the attention dilution inherent in flat retrieval systems.
75: 
76: ## **Integration within the Google Antigravity Harness**
77: 
78: Google Antigravity provides a robust, agent-first development harness characterized by its use of Model Context Protocol servers, secure terminal sandboxing, and background subagent orchestration. Packaging the memory system as an Antigravity plugin ensures seamless distribution and deep integration into the developer's native workflow.  
79: An Antigravity plugin is a self-contained deployable asset structured around a manifest file, alongside optional components such as taught skills, behavioral rules, and deterministic lifecycle hooks. The operational logic of the memory system relies extensively on this hook architecture, which permits custom scripts to intercept and modify the agent's execution loop at critical junctures.  
80: Upon the initiation of a new task, the session start hook activates. It executes a lightweight query against the local SQLite index to retrieve the highest-relevance architectural abstracts and global project guidelines, injecting them directly into the initial system prompt to ground the agent immediately. Before the agent is permitted to execute commands that modify the codebase—such as file replacement operations—a pre-tool use hook forces a just-in-time validation check. This step queries the memory index to ensure no established project rules or known failure modes are being violated by the proposed change.  
81: Following the completion of a task, a post-tool use hook triggers the extraction and reflection loop. Instead of blocking the primary conversational thread, the harness leverages its native subagent capabilities. A background subagent is invoked to evaluate the task trajectory using the Reflexion pattern. This specialized subagent analyzes the actions taken, identifies any novel solutions, dead-ends, or architectural shifts, and autonomously distills these insights into a new Markdown experience card, seamlessly committing it to the repository without interrupting the user.
82: 
83: ### **Validation, Expiry, and CI/CD Integration**
84: 
85: A memory system is only as reliable as its data freshness. As repositories undergo heavy refactoring, code citations and file paths within memory artifacts inevitably degrade. To manage this entropy, the plugin implements rigorous validation. Before an agent acts upon a retrieved memory, a background verification process checks the embedded citations against the current Git working tree. If the underlying code has shifted or the file no longer exists, the memory is flagged as stale and is either updated or ignored.  
86: Furthermore, procedural facts are subject to deterministic decay. Metrics such as the date of last use and total usage count are embedded in the Markdown frontmatter of each experience card. A cleanup script, executed on a schedule via the Antigravity scheduling tool, evaluates these metrics. Unused or severely outdated procedural memories are automatically archived or explicitly marked as superseded, preventing them from improperly influencing future context generation.  
87: To extend this intelligence beyond the local integrated development environment, the plugin interfaces directly with continuous integration and continuous delivery systems. Through the Harness Model Context Protocol server integration, the Antigravity agent can inspect deployment pipelines, correlate failed runs with local code changes, and update its memory with real-time deployment constraints, ensuring the agent's knowledge graph accurately reflects the entire software delivery lifecycle.
88: 
89: ## **Security Governance: Mitigating Memory and Context Poisoning**
90: 
91: As autonomous agents gain deeper access to enterprise systems and rely more heavily on persistent memory, they become highly vulnerable to a critical threat vector formally recognized as ASI06: Memory and Context Poisoning. Designing a repository-level memory system without robust defense mechanisms against this threat is a severe architectural failure.
92: 
93: ### **The Threat of Contextual Contamination**
94: 
95: Unlike transient prompt injection attacks—which generally end the moment the session closes and the context window is cleared—memory poisoning constitutes a delayed, persistent, and highly insidious attack. If an agent mistakenly ingests a malicious instruction via a compromised external dependency, a rogue pull request, or a manipulated third-party API payload, and subsequently distills that instruction into its permanent Markdown memory, the payload crosses the threshold into trusted ground truth.  
96: Because agents exhibit implicit trust in their own retrieved memories, this contamination is uniquely dangerous. Days or weeks after the initial injection, an entirely different developer might trigger a routine task that retrieves the poisoned experience card. The agent will then execute the malicious payload—potentially exfiltrating sensitive environment variables or hijacking a deployment pipeline—long after the attacker has vanished. Furthermore, systems are susceptible to bootstrap poisoning, a scenario where an agent hallucinates a false constraint, commits it to memory, and then continuously reinforces its own hallucination in a destructive, self-amplifying feedback loop.
97: 
98: ### **Defensive Architecture: Pre-Admission and Retrieval Screening**
99: 
100: To secure the Antigravity plugin, the memory architecture must implement rigorous defense-in-depth principles akin to the MemSentry or AM-Sentry frameworks. These frameworks shift the security posture from reactive patching to persistent governance.  
101: The primary defense mechanism is a structured pre-admission evaluation pipeline. The background distillation subagent must act as an adversarial reviewer. Before writing a new experience card to the file system, it evaluates the proposed memory against immutable, hardcoded security rules defined in the project's foundational configuration. The evaluation model calculates a security delta; operations that propose altering deployment scripts, manipulating access controls, or establishing unauthorized network connections receive a high-risk score. These flagged memories are strictly quarantined and require explicit human approval via the Antigravity user interface before they can be committed to the repository.  
102: Additionally, provenance tagging is strictly enforced. Every Markdown memory file must include cryptographic or structural metadata detailing its exact origin, specifying whether it was generated by a direct user prompt, synthesized from a specific internal file, or extracted from an external API payload. During the retrieval phase, the hybrid search engine dynamically filters out memories lacking proper provenance or those whose origins exhibit a low trust weight for the specific, sensitive task at hand, ensuring that untrusted external inputs cannot easily overwrite secure internal protocols.
103: 
104: ## **Evaluation Metrics and Benchmarking**
105: 
106: To ensure the memory plugin maintains high fidelity and does not succumb to context rot or poisoning over long operational horizons, its performance must be continuously evaluated against stringent industry benchmarks. Standard retrieval metrics, such as simple recall rates, are highly insufficient for agentic memory, as they only test static lookup capabilities and fail to measure dynamic reasoning.  
107: Production readiness is verified against comprehensive evaluation paradigms established by benchmarks designed specifically for long-term conversational and interactive memory.
108: 
109: | Benchmark Suite | Primary Task Focus | Key Evaluation Metrics | Value for Agentic Memory Assessment |
110: | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
111: | LoCoMo | Conversational recall across extended sessions | Retrieval accuracy, temporal reasoning | Tests basic long-term recall over hundreds of turns; highlights temporal disambiguation weaknesses. |
112: | LongMemEval | Interactive chat assistant memory | Multi-hop reasoning, recall under distraction | Simulates realistic production chat scenarios; measures ability to maintain accuracy as interaction depth grows. |
113: | BEAM | Interference, updates, and long-horizon tasks | Robustness to updates, event ordering | Critical for testing conflict resolution; evaluates how systems handle revised facts and entity interference at massive token scales (1M \- 10M tokens). |
114: | MemoryArena | Agentic task execution and planning | Task effectiveness, plan completion | Shifts focus from simple recall to evaluating memory coherence under operational pressure in multi-session workflows. |
115: 
116: A functional memory agent must demonstrate competency across four distinct pillars: accurate retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding, and conflict resolution. Temporal coherence and conflict resolution are particularly critical. If an architectural decision record from January mandates the use of one specific framework, and a subsequent record from March mandates a transition to a different framework, the retrieval engine must not only fetch the most recent fact but successfully map the invalidation of the obsolete fact. Event-centric memory architectures score significantly higher on these temporal conflict resolutions, showcasing the necessity of structured updates.  
117: Ultimately, the defining metric for the Antigravity plugin is the accuracy-latency frontier. The system must prove that it can achieve high multi-hop reasoning accuracy—synthesizing disparate project facts into a coherent action plan—while injecting a highly constrained number of tokens into the prompt window, thereby preserving both computational speed and financial efficiency.
118: 
119: ## **Synthesis and Strategic Recommendations**
120: 
121: Architecting an autonomous, repository-level memory system for Google Antigravity requires abandoning legacy approaches that rely on monolithic conversation buffers or heavy, cloud-based graph databases. The optimal path forward balances rigorous token efficiency, operational simplicity, and stringent security governance.  
122: The system must adopt a Markdown-canonical, Git-backed substrate. Storing all memory artifacts as plain text files in a dedicated directory guarantees zero vendor lock-in, immediate portability across developer machines, and native version control tracking, allowing human engineers to audit and govern the agent's knowledge base easily.  
123: To handle retrieval without external infrastructure, the architecture must utilize an embedded indexing engine. Embedding the pure-C sqlite-vec extension directly within the Antigravity plugin achieves sub-50ms hybrid search capabilities, ensuring lightning-fast access to relevant context without requiring developers to provision or maintain complex vector infrastructure.  
124: Efficiency is maintained through distillation-first write loops. By leveraging Antigravity's subagent capabilities to run background reflection tasks at the close of sessions, the system prevents context rot. It extracts only load-bearing facts, discards conversational static, and ensures that memory writes scale linearly rather than quadratically. This must be paired with hierarchical context injection, injecting only compact summaries at session start and allowing the agent to lazily load deeper context via tool calls only when analytically necessary.  
125: Finally, strict memory governance is non-negotiable. Treating the memory store as a high-value attack surface and implementing pre-admission validation hooks sanitizes distilled facts before they are written to disk. This prevents malicious context, prompt injections, or autonomous hallucinations from permanently poisoning the agent's baseline knowledge, ensuring the long-term integrity and reliability of the AI-assisted software development lifecycle.
126:

1: # Repo Memory: Specification
2: 
3: | | |
4: |---|---|
5: | **Status** | Draft v0.10 (see Revision history) |
6: | **Date** | 2026-09-30 |
7: | **Scope** | Repository-level memory for coding agents. **Release 1: Antigravity. Release 2: Claude Code.** Text marked **[R2]** belongs to Release 2; Release 1 is built so that Release 2 is an adapter, not a rewrite (§18.6). |
8: | **Implementation** | One Go binary, `repo-memory` (§18) |
9: | **Reference repo** | `esp32-app-foundation` (evidence in Appendix A) |
10: | **Supersedes** | `repo-memory-plugin-architecture-analysis.md` (annotated critique kept for the record) |
11: 
12: ---
13: 
14: ## 1. Purpose
15: 
16: An agent starting work on a large, long-lived repository should behave as if it had been on the project from day one. It should know how each part of the system works and why. It should know what invariants must hold and what has already been tried and failed. It should know what a given error usually means and how to verify a change on real hardware.
17: 
18: This specification defines a memory system that provides that knowledge:
19: 
20: - **automatically**, without the working agent spending tokens to record it;
21: - **efficiently**, delivering only what the current task, file, error or action needs;
22: - **accurately**, keeping each fact tied to the code and evidence it depends on;
23: - **completely**, covering every part of the system, including stable parts nobody has touched for months.
24: 
25: ### 1.1 Goals
26: 
27: | # | Goal |
28: |---|---|
29: | G1 | The working agent writes no memory. All capture and distillation is done by a background sidecar. |
30: | G2 | Every subsystem in the repo has memory coverage, whether or not a conversation has discussed it. |
31: | G3 | Knowledge is delivered at the moment of need (task start, file touch, error, risky action), not only on request. |
32: | G4 | A fact stays valid until something it depends on changes. Age and lack of use never retire knowledge. |
33: | G5 | Trust is earned from outcomes (tests, builds, flash logs, merges, human confirmation), never from retrieval frequency or self-rated confidence. |
34: | G6 | Memory is rebuildable. Improving the pipeline and re-running it over the full history improves all past memory. |
35: | G7 | Knowledge that lives in git is human-readable, reviewable per fact, and merge-safe. |
36: | G8 | The system measures its own effectiveness using signals every session produces. |
37: | G9 | Existing artefacts (PA workspaces, ADRs, design specs, commit history) can be ingested without a special migration path. |
38: 
39: ### 1.2 Non-goals
40: 
41: - Generic chat or personal-assistant memory (user preferences across unrelated projects).
42: - Replacing git, the issue tracker or human-facing documentation. Memory can *feed* documentation (§7.3) but doesn't own it.
43: - A graph database, cloud vector store or any server infrastructure.
44: - Autonomous commits to the user's working branches.
45: - Storing what can be derived cheaply from the code at read time (structure, signatures, call graphs).
46: 
47: ---
48: 
49: ## 2. Design principles
50: 
51: | # | Principle | Consequence |
52: |---|---|---|
53: | P1 | **Separate working from remembering.** | The main agent only works. Capture uses hooks (no LLM). Distillation happens asynchronously in the sidecar. |
54: | P2 | **Event-sourced knowledge.** | Sessions, commits, human reviews and imported documents are immutable *events*. Knowledge is a *projection* over events and can be recomputed. |
55: | P3 | **Store only what the code can't tell you.** | Memory holds intent, rationale, ruled-out approaches, failure signatures, hardware and library behaviour, verified procedures, conventions and decisions. Structure is read from the code. |
56: | P4 | **The claim is the unit of knowledge.** | Knowledge is stored as small, typed, evidence-backed claims anchored to code. Documents are generated *views* over claims. |
57: | P5 | **Truth from outcomes.** | A claim's status comes from evidence in the trace (tool results, test outcomes, merges, reverts, human statements), not from the agent's prose. Hypotheses remain hypotheses. |
58: | P6 | **Code is the index.** | Entities are derived from the repository. Retrieval is keyed on the code the agent is touching, the errors it sees and the task text, not on embedding similarity over the opening prompt. |
59: | P7 | **Validity follows dependencies.** | Claims are re-checked when their anchored code, library versions, toolchain or config change. Nothing expires with time or disuse. |
60: | P8 | **Push, with a strict budget.** | Hot-path delivery is deterministic, bounded in tokens and deduplicated per session. Only high-trust claims are pushed. |
61: | P9 | **Humans are the highest authority.** | Human statements and reviews are events with the highest trust. The system asks targeted questions to fill rationale gaps. |
62: | P10 | **Harness-agnostic core, thin adapters.** | Pipeline, stores and views are plain files plus SQLite. There is no custom daemon or socket. Antigravity (Release 1) and Claude Code (Release 2) are adapters behind one interface. Delivery is chosen by each harness's declared *capabilities*, never by its name (§18.3). |
63: | P11 | **Never slow the loop.** | Hooks run synchronously and block the agent. Hook scripts only read precomputed files and indexes. All LLM work happens in the tick. |
64: | P12 | **Review gates sharing, not use.** | A developer's own machine uses new claims as soon as they reach `verified`. Review controls what enters the shared repository. |
65: | P13 | **Evidence must be independent of the memory it supports.** | Only tool outcomes and human-authored messages are evidence; agent text never is. Anything a session was shown by memory (its *exposure*) cannot come back as support for the same claim unless a new outcome actually tested it (§6.6). This prevents memory from reinforcing itself through the sessions it informs, including bug-fixer sessions and report conversations. |
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. Terminology
70: 
71: | Term | Meaning |
72: |---|---|
73: | **Session** | One agent conversation, including any subagent sessions it spawned. |
74: | **Raw transcript** | The harness's native record of a session (Antigravity conversation DB, Claude Code JSONL). |
75: | **Episode** | The compacted, scrubbed, harness-neutral record of a session produced by the pipeline (§5.1). |
76: | **Event** | Any immutable input to the knowledge projection: an episode, a commit, a human review decision, a human answer, or an imported document. |
77: | **Entity** | A thing claims are about: a code element (subsystem, file, symbol, config key, build env, topic, MCP tool, error string) or an external element (library@version, SDK version, board, tool). |
78: | **Anchor** | A reference from a claim to an entity, carrying a fingerprint of the anchored content. |
79: | **Claim** | A typed, evidence-backed statement about one or more entities (§5.3). |
80: | **View** | A generated document rendered from claims and entities (§5.5). |
81: | **Claim index** | A generated view listing, per subsystem, each pushable claim's ID and `relevant_when` line, so an agent can find relevant claims itself with ordinary file reads (§5.5). |
82: | **Memory artefact** | A file a working agent or the PA writes to record knowledge (PA `MEMORY.md`, `PROJECT.md` session logs, completion reports, a harness-native memory store). Writes to one are a triage signal (§6.4). |
83: | **Event path** | Work started by a harness hook. Knows exactly which session changed, must return in milliseconds, and only reads, injects and writes spool files (§4.1). |
84: | **Time path** | Work started by a scheduled tick. Does all asynchronous work (§4.1). |
85: | **Sidecar** | An Antigravity-managed scheduled job: a periodic tick, not a daemon. |
86: | **Tick** | One scheduled run of `repo-memory tick`. It advances pending jobs within a time budget, then exits. |
87: | **Job** | A durable unit of asynchronous work in the job table (§4.3), advanced step by step across ticks. |
88: | **Housekeeping run** | A headless `agy -p` call made by the pipeline, on the user's Antigravity quota. Not visible in the IDE (§4.4). |
89: | **Report** | An IDE-visible conversation (`agentapi`) that the tick starts for the human, only when there is something worth reviewing (§4.4). |
90: | **Trigger** | A runtime condition that causes knowledge to be delivered to the working agent (§7). |
91: | **Exposure** | A session receiving memory content: pushed by a hook, returned by a pull tool, or read directly from `.memory/`. Recorded per step in the episode (§5.1) and used to enforce P13. |
92: | **Salience window** | A range of episode steps selected mechanically around failures, fixes, reverts, human decisions and trade-off reasoning. Extraction reads windows rather than whole episodes (§6.4). |
93: 
94: ---
95: 
96: ## 4. Architecture overview
97: 
98: ```
99:           EVENT PATH (hooks)                               TIME PATH (scheduled tick, every minute)
100:   ┌──────── Working agent (Antigravity / Claude Code) ─────────┐
101:   │  works normally — writes no memory                         │
102:   │  ▲ push: brief · touch · error · risky action · déjà-vu    │
103:   │  │ pull: ask / why / history / brief / note / stats ───────┼──▶ MCP server ──▶ agy -p (synchronous)
104:   └──┼───────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘
105:      │ inline        │ Stop · PreInvocation · PreToolUse · PostToolUse
106:      │ (no LLM)      ▼ write spool files only
107:      │        ┌─────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
108:      │        │   spool/    │──────▶ │ Tick: ingest spool → job table → next steps   │
109:      │        └─────────────┘        │  • mechanical work in-process                 │
110:      │                               │  • LLM steps: agy -p child processes          │
111:      │                               │    (headless housekeeping; waited, bounded)   │
112:      │                               │  • reports: agentapi (visible in the IDE)     │
113:      │                               │  • sweep, git checks, calendar jobs           │
114:      │                               └───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
115:      │                                                       ▼
116:      │          1 Compact → 2 Triage → 3 Extract → 4 Reconcile → 5 Verify → 6 Publish
117:      │             │                             │                          │
118:      │             ▼                             ▼                          ▼
119:      │     Episode log (private)   Claim store (git) + entity skeleton   Views (generated)
120:      │                                           │                          │
